SURVEY_TYPE: Casual observation from kayaking and snorkeling over the past weeks
SOURCE: Paul Barker, Paul.barker@global.net.pg. Date of observation: Successive weeks since mid-December.latest today (25th January 2009) only snorkeling so not quite sure of depth.
COMMENTS:
About 35% of hard corals and similar portions of soft corals bleached in later Dec, but early Jan much more bleached, and now (25th Jan) a similar portion of coral (and many species of Anemone)are bleached but many of the December bleached corals now seem to be dead or partly dead, and with algae starting to grow over them. So cumulatively it seems the majority in the shallows is either bleached or was bleached in late Dec/early Jan and is now dead or partly dead. Bleaching started around mid-3rd week December 08. I’ve observed on coastal reefs and off several nearby islands, but understand it also prevails some way down the coast at least in the inner islands (I’ve not checked the outer reef nor greater depths). 3rd week of December - mostly alive (80% perhaps).

Now much less is alive and even large reef forming corals seem to have died..

SOURCE: Ilsa kuffner, Coral Reef Ecologist, US Geological Survey (ikuffner@usgs.gov)

COMMENTS: I have just been informed by Croy McCoy that they are having an intense and widespread bleaching event in Grand Cayman. He went diving yesterday and found totally bleached corals down to 30 m, observations indicate that close to 100% of scleractinians showed bleaching signs in deeper environments, and around 80% in shallower habitats. Water temps. Have been above 29 Celcius since June (Hobo data). I will be conducting disease surveys in mid-November, so if anything like what we saw in 2005 with WPD and YBD outbreaks during and after the massive bleaching occurs here, we will probably have a chance to document this in our permanent survey transects around the island. Croy will be conducting quantitative surveys and tagging colonies in the next days. On the other hand, here in Puerto Rico, there are no signs of a bleaching event. Just the usual, a few pale colonies here and there. Same situation observed during our disease surveys last week in Grenada.

SOURCE: MC. Rosa Rodríguez-Martínez Lab. Sistemas Arrecifales Unidad Académica de Sistemas Arrecifales ICMyL, UNAM Puerto Morelos, Q. Roo, México Tel. 52 (998) 87 102 19 xt. 128 Fax. 52 (998) 87 101 38 [Coral-List] Bleaching in the Mexican Caribbean (Fri 9/25/2009 11:37 PM)
COMMENTS: An intense bleaching event is also occurring along the Mexican Caribbean Coast. Our first observations of pale corals was done in May in Akumal reef, with 7% of the colonies showing pale coloration at a depth of 10-15m. By June, 9% of the colonies were bleached-pale in Mahahual Reef at the same depth. By July, 32% of the colonies were bleached-pale in Punta Allen reef. At present, (August-September) surveys at Puerto Morelos reef show that 41% of the colonies were bleached and 31% of them were completely white. Surveys were done at a depth of 4-8m. The number of colonies sampled at each site was over 2000. Almost all scleractinian species showed bleaching signs, as well as some gorgonians, Milleporas and zoanthids.

COMMENTS: From 2014-2017, during our routine vessel patrols across the marine park, there were only very very occasional observations of very minor and isolated bleaching. Similarly, during the same period there were only very occasional reports of very minor and isolated bleaching from the tourism industry and these were unverified. No widespread bleaching was observed or reported from 2014-2017. Aerial surveys flown at 1000ft covered the entire length of Ningaloo Marine Park from Exmouth Gulf to Red Bluff including the Muiron Islands. SOURCE: University of Guam Marine Laboratory, David  Burdick, David  Burdick burdickdr@hotmail.com
CITATION: UOGML, unpublished data; Burdick, D., Raymundo, L., Reynolds, T., Miller, R., Gault, J.
COMMENTS: The PERCENT_BLEACHED values represent the percentage of coral cover that was pale or bleached and the PERCENT_MORTALITY values represent the percentage of coral cover that was recently killed as a result of coral bleaching. Most sites surveyed in 2015 were visited prior to the warmest months, but a few were surveyed in September when bleaching would be expected. We observed only very minor paling/bleaching in 2015 and provide this data rather than reply simply on anecdotal reports. The 2015 surveys were carred out at a random subset of the sites surveyed in 2013, with the intent being to assess the cumulative mortality associated with bleaching in 2013 and 2014, the latter of which we have very limited data for. It's important to note that the windward east coast of Guam was significantly under-sampled in 2015, 2016, and 2017 as a result of hazardous water conditions, whereas in 2013 we were able to visit several sites along the east coast. East coast sites generally had higher coverage of bleaching-susceptible species in 2013, and so were impacted more severely than the leeward west coast sites. Thus, rates of bleaching and associated mortality in 2017 especially, likely represent an underestimate of rates island-wide.

SOURCE: University of Guam Marine Laboratory, David  Burdick, David  Burdick burdickdr@hotmail.com
CITATION: UOGML, unpublished data; Burdick, D., Idechong, I., Gault, J.
COMMENTS: The PERCENT_BLEACHED values represent the percentage of coral cover that was pale, bleached, or dead from bleaching and the PERCENT_MORTALITY values represent the percentage of coral cover that was dead as a result of coral bleaching. Similar to the 2015 survey effort, most sites surveyed in 2016 were visited prior to the warmest months, but a few were surveyed in September when bleaching would be expected. And, as in 2015, we observed only very minor paling/bleaching in 2016--at least on the seaward slope ("forereef")-- and provide this data rather than reply simply on anecdotal reports (bleaching was reported from the reef flat--see data provided by Whitney Hoot). The 2016 surveys were carried out as part of a NOAA S-K grant-funded reef resilience assessment. An effort was made to visit sites previously visited in 2013 and 2015 (or at least just 2013); however, a few sites were added to this effort that had not been surveyed previously. The general location of these additional sites (RR-1, RR-3, and RR-4) was determined in a non-random manner, with the intent of achieving a somewhat regular spacing of sites along Guam's coastline; the exact location of the sites was selected haphazardly using GIS. It's important to note that the windward east coast of Guam was significantly under-sampled in 2015, 2016, and 2017 as a result of hazardous water conditions, whereas in 2013 we were able to visit several sites along the east coas. East coast sites generally had higher coverage of bleaching-susceptible species in 2013, and so were impacted more severely than the leeward west coast sites. Thus, rates of bleaching and associated mortality in 2017 especially, likely represent an underestimate of rates island-wide.

COMMENTS: The PERCENT_BLEACHED values represent the percentage of observed coral colonies that were pale, bleached (including colonies with partial mortality that were bleached) and the PERCENT_MORTALITY values represent the percentage of observed colonies that were partially or wholly dead as a result of coral bleaching (including colonies that were counted as pale or bleached that had partial mortality). Because the percentage of pale/bleached colonies includes colonies that had partial mortality associated with bleaching, and those colonies are also counted in the percent mortality value, combining these values would result in an overestimate of total bleaching impact. It's important to note that the windward east coast of Guam was significantly under-sampled in 2015, 2016, and 2017 as a result of hazardous water conditions, whereas in 2013 we were able to visit several sites along the east coas. East coast sites generally had higher coverage of bleaching-susceptible species in 2013, and so were impacted more severely than the leeward west coast sites. Thus, rates of bleaching and associated mortality in 2017 especially, likely represent an underestimate of rates island-wide. We have percent cover data but unfortunately I was unable to QC it in time to include here, so rather than provide no data for the 2017 event, which was of greater magnitude (in terms of DHW) than the 2013 event, I thought I would provide our colony-based data. I should add that based on experience the colony-level percent bleaching and mortality rates are often higher than percent cover based values, so care must be taken when comparing the 2017 data to other years. I can try to get the 2017 percent cover data to you by early next week, as I need to do that anyway for a Guam-focused paper, but my plans may be foiled by an approaching storm that is expected to reach typhoon status by the time it reaches us in a few days(!)
